children: Falling oil prices and a recovering rupee are boosting the appeal of Indian government bonds to foreign investors, after inflows topped $1 billion this month, data from the Clearing Corporation of India showed.
The rupee's rebound is easing concerns that currency losses could erode bond returns, while cheaper oil is supporting both the currency and debt.

Indian government bonds offer an increasingly attractive medium-term opportunity as valuations have improved materially, said Norbert Ling, Invesco's head of fixed income portfolio management for Asia-Pacific.
Ling said he favours seven- to eight-year bonds for their balance of interest income and sensitivity to yield movements, as well as potential gains as yields decline when the bonds approach maturity.
Foreign investors have bought $1.1 billion worth of Indian government bonds this month, reversing three straight months of net selling.

Investors bought Indian government bonds at attractive valuations, lifting holdings of index-linked debt near two-month highs, though further purchases hinge on US Treasury yields, the dollar, oil prices and RBI policy.

A spike in oil prices through October and a relatively hawkish Reserve Bank of India had pushed the 10-year benchmark government bond yield to almost 7.50%, a level which has attracted value investors.

"The benchmark bond yield had recently crossed levels last seen in late 2022, proving exciting enough for foreign investors to turn large bond buyers, and more flows could be seen, if there is any possibility of a quick and swift resolution to the US-Iran war," said Pranab Sarkar, head of securities trading at Sun Global.
Brent crude prices are trading around $92 per barrel, down 23% from peak hit at October-end.
Sarkar said he prefers to stick to the most liquid part of the curve in the form of the 10-year security.
Foreign inflows in November have been led by seven-year and 10-year securities, which have cornered over half of the total purchases.
